entries.meaning: To hold and control a climbing rope for a partner, or, at sea, to make a line fast around a cleat — and in Navy usage, to cancel an order.
examples: Always belay your partner before they leave the ground.
She belayed me on every pitch of the route.
He has belayed for beginners at the gym for six years.
By noon they had belayed each other up four routes.
The bosun belays the halyard to a pin on the rail.
They belayed the line and let the sail hold.
The crew had belayed every sheet before the squall hit.
Belay that — we're taking the other truck.
Belay my last transmission; the coordinates were wrong.

senses.head: Belay a climber
body: The everyday modern sense: to manage the rope so that a partner's fall is caught. Fully regular in American English — belayed, never the old ✗ belaid. (страховать (в альпинизме))
examples: Always belay your partner before they leave the ground.
She belayed me on every pitch of the route.
He has belayed for beginners at the gym for six years.
By noon they had belayed each other up four routes.

senses.head: Make a rope fast (nautical)
body: At sea: to secure a line by winding it around a cleat or a belaying pin. This is the original sense, and the archaic past belaid belongs to it. (закреплять (канат, снасть))
examples: The bosun belays the halyard to a pin on the rail.
They belayed the line and let the sail hold.
The crew had belayed every sheet before the squall hit.

senses.head: Belay that! — cancel an order
body: Navy and Coast Guard usage, and it exists only as an imperative — there is no past tense in practice. Belay that means disregard what was just said. (отставить!, отменить (приказ))
examples: Belay that — we're taking the other truck.
Belay my last transmission; the coordinates were wrong.

entries.forms: belay /bɪˈleɪ/ · belayed /bɪˈleɪd/ · belayed /bɪˈleɪd/ — the older nautical belaid /bɪˈleɪd/ is the form the source list records
entries.register: rare — a climbing and sailing term; outside those trades Americans meet it only in the Navy's Belay that!
entries.contrast: This is the odd one out among the -lay verbs here. Lay, mislay and overlay all give -laid, but belay went regular centuries ago: modern American English says belayed, and every climbing manual prints it that way. Belaid survives only in old sailing texts. Note also the Navy idiom Belay that!, meaning "cancel that" — it has no past tense at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: managing a rope (belay your partner), making a line fast (belay the halyard), and the Navy imperative Belay that!, which exists only as a command.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a climber or a line as object (she belayed me on every pitch), intransitive when the partner is understood (he has belayed for beginners for six years).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — I was belayed by my partner on every pitch; the halyard is belayed to a pin on the rail. The imperative Belay that! has no passive.

entries.meaning: To cut something short with scissors or clippers, to cut a piece out of print, to fasten with a clip, or to strike something a glancing blow.
examples: I clip the dog myself to save eighty dollars.
She clipped her nails over the trash can.
The barber has clipped his hair the same way since 1998.
We had clipped the hedge back before the storm came through.
My grandmother still clips recipes out of the Sunday paper.
He clipped the obituary and mailed it to me.
Fans have clipped the best thirty seconds of the interview.
Clip the badge to your jacket before you go in.
The sound tech clipped a mic to his collar.
Someone had clipped the pages together in the wrong order.
If you clip the curb at that angle you'll blow a tire.
The truck clipped our mirror and kept going.
He has clipped the same doorframe twice this month.
The new rules clip the mayor's authority considerably.
Budget cuts clipped the program back to two days a week.
The board has clipped his wings since the merger.

senses.head: Cut with scissors or clippers
body: The core sense: trimming hair, nails, a hedge, or an animal's coat. Regular in modern usage; the poetic participle clipt is dead. (стричь, подрезать)
examples: I clip the dog myself to save eighty dollars.
She clipped her nails over the trash can.
The barber has clipped his hair the same way since 1998.
We had clipped the hedge back before the storm came through.

senses.head: Cut something out of print
body: To snip an article, coupon, or photo out of printed material — still alive in clip coupons. Extended now to saving a short piece of video or audio. (вырезать (из газеты, журнала))
examples: My grandmother still clips recipes out of the Sunday paper.
He clipped the obituary and mailed it to me.
Fans have clipped the best thirty seconds of the interview.

senses.head: Fasten with a clip
body: To attach one thing to another with a clip or clasp. The pattern is clip A to B. (прикреплять, пристёгивать)
examples: Clip the badge to your jacket before you go in.
The sound tech clipped a mic to his collar.
Someone had clipped the pages together in the wrong order.

senses.head: Hit with a glancing blow
body: To strike something in passing, usually by accident and usually at speed. Common in driving and in contact sports. (задеть, зацепить (вскользь))
examples: If you clip the curb at that angle you'll blow a tire.
The truck clipped our mirror and kept going.
He has clipped the same doorframe twice this month.

senses.head: Cut short, curtail
body: Figurative: to reduce or limit. Fixed in clip someone's wings, meaning restrict their freedom, and in clipped speech, meaning terse and brisk. (укорачивать, урезать, ограничивать)
examples: The new rules clip the mayor's authority considerably.
Budget cuts clipped the program back to two days a week.
The board has clipped his wings since the merger.

entries.forms: clip /klɪp/ · clipped /klɪpt/ · clipped /klɪpt/ — the archaic participle clipt /klɪpt/ is what the source list records
entries.register: everyday — clipping coupons, nails, or a curb is ordinary American conversation
entries.contrast: Clip is a fully regular verb in American English: clipped for both the past and the participle. Clipt is an old poetic spelling — Shakespeare and hymn books have it — and it sounds exactly the same, so nothing is lost by ignoring it. Do not write ✗ He has clipt the hedge today.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: cutting (clip the dog), snipping out of print (clip a coupon), fastening (clip the badge on), striking in passing (clip the curb), and figurative curtailing (clip his wings).
entries.transitivity: transitive in all five senses, and the object is normally obligatory — ✗ The truck clipped is incomplete. The fastening sense adds a goal phrase: clip A to B.
entries.passive: yes — his hair has been clipped the same way since 1998; a mic was clipped to his collar; his wings have been clipped since the merger.

entries.meaning: To deny or contradict something — formal, and almost always in a negative frame.
examples: No one can gainsay the numbers in her report.
The committee gainsaid every point he made.
Nobody has gainsaid the finding in twenty years.
Few of his officers dared gainsay him.
She gainsaid the bishop in open council.
Until last week no one had gainsaid the old theory.

senses.head: Deny, contradict a statement
body: Formal and largely written. It lives in negative frames — no one can gainsay it, there is no gainsaying it — and sounds wrong in a plain positive sentence. (отрицать, оспаривать)
examples: No one can gainsay the numbers in her report.
The committee gainsaid every point he made.
Nobody has gainsaid the finding in twenty years.

senses.head: Oppose, speak against someone
body: With a person or an authority as the object: to speak in open opposition to them. Archaic in tone and rare outside legal or literary prose. (противоречить, перечить (кому-л.))
examples: Few of his officers dared gainsay him.
She gainsaid the bishop in open council.
Until last week no one had gainsaid the old theory.

entries.forms: gainsay /ˌɡeɪnˈseɪ/ · gainsaid /ˌɡeɪnˈsɛd/ · gainsaid /ˌɡeɪnˈsɛd/ — the spelling pronunciation /ˌɡeɪnˈseɪd/ is also accepted for the past and participle
entries.register: rare — formal and nearly frozen in no one can gainsay it; almost never produced in speech
entries.contrast: The past follows said, so it is normally /ˌɡeɪnˈsɛd/, rhyming with bed; the spelling pronunciation /ˌɡeɪnˈseɪd/ is also heard and accepted. The third person, though, keeps the /eɪ/ — gainsays is not pronounced like says /sɛz/. Note too that this verb is formal and lives almost entirely in negative frames: no one can gainsay it, not ✗ I gainsay you.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of speech, but so formal and frozen that it barely appears outside negative frames: no one can gainsay it, there is no gainsaying it.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — a statement (gainsay the numbers) or a person (gainsay the bishop). ✗ Nobody gainsaid is incomplete.
entries.passive: restricted — natural only in the negative frames the verb lives in: the finding has not been gainsaid in twenty years. A plain positive passive sounds wrong: ✗ Every point was gainsaid by the committee.

entries.meaning: To possess or hold something; to eat, experience, receive, or arrange something; and, as an auxiliary, to build every perfect tense in English.
examples: We have two cars and no garage.
They had a house on the lake before the divorce.
She has had that jacket since college.
They have finished the roof already.
By the time we sat down, they had eaten.
She has had three interviews this week.
I usually have oatmeal before a run.
We had pizza twice last week.
He has had nothing but coffee all day.
Did you have a good flight?
I had a headache all afternoon.
She has had a rough year.
We have a staff meeting every Monday at nine.
They had a barbecue for the whole street.
The club has had the same fundraiser for twelve years.
You have to show ID at the door.
I had to leave before the second half.
We have had to rewrite the contract twice.
I have got a meeting at three I can't move.
You have got to see this.
She has got two brothers in Chicago.
I'll have the office send you the file.
We had the roof replaced last spring.
She has had her hair cut short since June.
She's going to have a baby in March.
Our cat had five kittens under the porch.
They have had three children in five years.
May I have your attention for a moment?
We had word from the embassy this morning.
I have had no answer from them at all.
I will not have shouting in this house.
The principal wouldn't have any of it.
They had enough sense not to argue with her about it.
If you paid full price for that, you have been had.
The dealer had us on the trade-in value.
They realized they had been had only after the check cleared.

senses.head: Possess, own
body: The basic full-verb sense. In informal American speech it usually appears as have got: I've got two brothers means the same as I have two brothers. (иметь, обладать)
examples: We have two cars and no garage.
They had a house on the lake before the divorce.
She has had that jacket since college.

senses.head: Auxiliary of the perfect tenses
body: Have/has + participle makes the present perfect, had + participle the past perfect. In speech it weakens to /əv/, which is why people misspell it ✗ would of gone for would have gone. (вспомогательный глагол перфекта)
examples: They have finished the roof already.
By the time we sat down, they had eaten.
She has had three interviews this week.

senses.head: Eat or drink something
body: Have replaces eat and drink in most ordinary sentences: you have lunch, a coffee, a beer. (есть, пить, принимать (пищу))
examples: I usually have oatmeal before a run.
We had pizza twice last week.
He has had nothing but coffee all day.

senses.head: Experience, undergo
body: Used of illnesses, feelings, and things that happen to you: have a headache, have a good time, have an accident. (испытывать, переживать)
examples: Did you have a good flight?
I had a headache all afternoon.
She has had a rough year.

senses.head: Hold an event; take part in one
body: Have a party, a meeting, a conversation, an argument — the subject organizes it or is in it. (устраивать, проводить)
examples: We have a staff meeting every Monday at nine.
They had a barbecue for the whole street.
The club has had the same fundraiser for twelve years.

senses.head: Have to — be obliged
body: Have to + base verb expresses obligation, and it is what English uses in the past, where must has no form: I had to leave. In fast speech it becomes hafta. (быть должным, приходиться)
examples: You have to show ID at the door.
I had to leave before the second half.
We have had to rewrite the contract twice.

senses.head: Have got — informal possession and obligation
body: Spoken American English adds got: I've got a meeting (possession) and I've got to go (obligation, reduced to gotta). Present tense only — the past is plain had and had to. (разг.: иметь; быть должным)
examples: I have got a meeting at three I can't move.
You have got to see this.
She has got two brothers in Chicago.

senses.head: Have something done — causative
body: Have + object + participle means you arranged for someone else to do it: have the car fixed. With a bare infinitive — have someone do it — you are directing the person yourself. (поручать, делать (чужими руками))
examples: I'll have the office send you the file.
We had the roof replaced last spring.
She has had her hair cut short since June.

senses.head: Give birth to
body: Of people and animals alike: have a baby, have puppies. Neutral, and by far the commonest way to say it. (рожать, родить)
examples: She's going to have a baby in March.
Our cat had five kittens under the porch.
They have had three children in five years.

senses.head: Receive, get
body: Somewhat formal or written: have news, have word from someone, may I have your attention. (получать)
examples: May I have your attention for a moment?
We had word from the embassy this morning.
I have had no answer from them at all.

senses.head: Allow, tolerate
body: Negative only, and emphatic: I won't have it, she wouldn't have any of that. It means refuse to permit. (терпеть, допускать)
examples: I will not have shouting in this house.
The principal wouldn't have any of it.
They had enough sense not to argue with her about it.

senses.head: Be had — be cheated
body: Usually passive: you've been had means you were tricked or overcharged. British have someone on means to tease them; Americans say put someone on. (быть обманутым, попасться на удочку)
examples: If you paid full price for that, you have been had.
The dealer had us on the trade-in value.
They realized they had been had only after the check cleared.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking, and the auxiliary behind every perfect tense
entries.third person: has /hæz/ (not ✗ haves) · -ing form: having (drop the e)
entries.contrast: Have is both a full verb and the auxiliary that builds every perfect tense, so the two stack: I have had three cups of coffee, she had had enough. In speech the auxiliary weakens to /əv/, which sounds exactly like of — that is why people write ✗ would of gone. It is always would have gone or would've gone. Also watch the contraction 'd, which can be either had or would: I'd finished is had, I'd finish is would.
entries.verb type: stative in the core senses — possession (we have two cars), experience (I had a headache), obligation (have to) — and there it rejects the progressive: ✗ I am having two cars. Dynamic in the eat/drink, hold-an-event, give-birth and causative senses, where the progressive is fine: we're having lunch, she's having a baby. Also the auxiliary behind every perfect tense (they have finished).
entries.transitivity: transitive in every full-verb sense, object obligatory — ✗ We have is incomplete. The causative takes object + complement: have the roof replaced, have the office send you the file. Never ditransitive. As auxiliary it takes no object at all, only a participle.
entries.passive: no for the stative senses — this is the classic learner trap: ✗ Two cars are had by us, ✗ A headache was had by me, ✗ A meeting is had every Monday. The auxiliary has no passive either. The one live passive is the fixed idiom be had 'be cheated': if you paid full price, you have been had.
entries.phrasal verbs: have at · have in · have it in for · have it out · have on · have over

entries.meaning: To set pieces of one material into the surface of another so that the finished surface stays flush.
examples: Craftsmen still inlay mother-of-pearl by hand in that shop.
The luthier inlaid tiny stars along the neck of the guitar.
Someone has inlaid brass letters into the lobby floor.
By 1890 the builders had inlaid every door in the house with ivory.
This dentist inlays gold in cases where a crown would be too much.
They inlaid porcelain rather than amalgam.
By the second visit he had inlaid both molars.

senses.head: Set material into a surface
body: Woodworking, jewelry, and instrument making: shell, metal, or stone let into wood or silver. The pattern is inlay A with B or inlay B into A. (инкрустировать, вкладывать)
examples: Craftsmen still inlay mother-of-pearl by hand in that shop.
The luthier inlaid tiny stars along the neck of the guitar.
Someone has inlaid brass letters into the lobby floor.
By 1890 the builders had inlaid every door in the house with ivory.

senses.head: Fit a dental inlay
body: Dentistry: to fit a shaped filling into a prepared cavity. Most people meet the noun an inlay, but the verb is standard in clinical writing. (ставить вкладку (в зуб))
examples: This dentist inlays gold in cases where a crown would be too much.
They inlaid porcelain rather than amalgam.
By the second visit he had inlaid both molars.

entries.register: rare — a craft and dental term; most Americans know only the noun an inlay
entries.contrast: Stress moves between the verb and the noun: the verb is in-LAY /ɪnˈleɪ/, but the noun — a piece of inlaid work, or a dental filling — is IN-lay /ˈɪnˌleɪ/. Everything else follows lay.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: setting one material flush into the surface of another (inlay mother-of-pearl by hand), including the dental sense (inlay gold).
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory, in two frames — inlay A with B (inlay the wood with brass) or inlay B into A (inlay brass into the floor).
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commoner form — every door in the house had been inlaid with ivory; brass letters have been inlaid into the lobby floor. The participle doubles as an adjective: an inlaid box.

entries.meaning: To put something down flat — and from there, to install, prepare, establish, impose, or wager it. Always transitive; the intransitive verb is lie.
examples: Please lay the baby in the crib on her back.
He laid his keys on the counter and forgot them there.
She has laid a blanket over him.
That turtle lays her eggs on the same beach every June.
The salmon laid their eggs and died.
The hens have laid six eggs this week.
They lay about four hundred feet of pipe a day.
We had laid the tile before the inspector arrived.
The crew has laid new cable down the whole street.
Lay the table for six, please.
He laid a fire in the grate before the guests arrived.
They had laid a trap and he walked right into it.
These three chapters lay the foundation for everything after.
That treaty laid the groundwork for forty years of peace.
Her early work has laid the basis for the whole field.
Don't lay the blame on the intern.
Prosecutors laid three charges against the company.
Two countries have laid claim to the same reef.
I'd lay money that he shows up late.
He laid fifty dollars on the underdog.
She has laid a small bet on every Derby since 1990.
Management may lay off more people after the audit.
The plant laid off two hundred workers in March.
They have laid off a third of the department since spring.
She lays out her clothes the night before every workday.
He laid out the whole proposal in fifteen minutes.
The memo has laid out exactly what happens next.
The coach lays down the same three rules every season.
The rebels laid down their arms at dawn.
The band has laid down four tracks this week.

senses.head: Put something down flat
body: The core sense, and it always takes an object. Do not confuse it with intransitive lie: ✗ I laid down for a nap should be I lay down for a nap. (класть, положить)
examples: Please lay the baby in the crib on her back.
He laid his keys on the counter and forgot them there.
She has laid a blanket over him.

senses.head: Lay eggs
body: Of birds, fish, and insects. It works without an object too: the hens aren't laying. (нести (яйца), откладывать яйца)
examples: That turtle lays her eggs on the same beach every June.
The salmon laid their eggs and died.
The hens have laid six eggs this week.

senses.head: Install, put in place
body: The building trades: lay tile, lay carpet, lay pipe, lay track, lay brick. (укладывать, прокладывать)
examples: They lay about four hundred feet of pipe a day.
We had laid the tile before the inspector arrived.
The crew has laid new cable down the whole street.

senses.head: Set out, prepare
body: Lay the table, lay a fire, lay a trap, lay plans. British English says lay the table where Americans usually say set the table. (накрывать (на стол); разводить (огонь); готовить (ловушку))
examples: Lay the table for six, please.
He laid a fire in the grate before the guests arrived.
They had laid a trap and he walked right into it.

senses.head: Lay a foundation, lay the groundwork
body: Figurative and very common in writing about projects and arguments: lay a foundation, lay the groundwork, lay the basis for. (закладывать (основу, фундамент))
examples: These three chapters lay the foundation for everything after.
That treaty laid the groundwork for forty years of peace.
Her early work has laid the basis for the whole field.

senses.head: Impose, assign (blame, charges, a tax)
body: Formal and legal: lay blame on someone, lay charges, lay claim to, lay a tax on. (возлагать (вину); налагать (обвинение, налог))
examples: Don't lay the blame on the intern.
Prosecutors laid three charges against the company.
Two countries have laid claim to the same reef.

senses.head: Bet, wager
body: Lay a bet, lay odds, lay money on something. Informal; I'd lay money that… just means the speaker is confident. (ставить (в пари), держать пари)
examples: I'd lay money that he shows up late.
He laid fifty dollars on the underdog.
She has laid a small bet on every Derby since 1990.

senses.head: Lay off — dismiss from a job
body: To end someone's employment for economic reasons rather than for cause — quite different from fire. Informally, lay off something also means quit doing it: lay off the coffee. (увольнять (по сокращению))
examples: Management may lay off more people after the audit.
The plant laid off two hundred workers in March.
They have laid off a third of the department since spring.

senses.head: Lay out — arrange, or explain in detail
body: Two everyday uses: spreading things out in order (lay out your clothes), and presenting a plan or an argument point by point (lay out the terms). (раскладывать, размещать; излагать)
examples: She lays out her clothes the night before every workday.
He laid out the whole proposal in fifteen minutes.
The memo has laid out exactly what happens next.

senses.head: Lay down — set a rule, or put aside
body: Lay down the law means state the rules firmly; lay down arms means surrender. In music, lay down a track means record it. (устанавливать (правила); складывать (оружие))
examples: The coach lays down the same three rules every season.
The rebels laid down their arms at dawn.
The band has laid down four tracks this week.

entries.register: everyday — you lay something down a dozen times a day without noticing
entries.contrast: This is the classic trap in English. Lay takes an object — you lay something down — and goes lay, laid, laid. Lie takes no object — you lie down yourself — and goes lie, lay, lain. The collision is that lay is also the past of lie: ✗ I laid down for a nap should be I lay down for a nap. And the spelling of the past is laid, never ✗ layed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from putting something down flat to installing (lay tile), preparing (lay a trap), imposing (lay blame), and wagering (lay fifty dollars).
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is what separates it from intransitive lie: ✗ I laid down for a nap should be I lay down for a nap. The one object-dropping sense is egg-laying: the hens aren't laying.
entries.passive: yes — the tile had been laid before the inspector arrived; three charges were laid against the company; two hundred workers were laid off in March.
entries.phrasal verbs: lay aside · lay away · lay down · lay in · lay into · lay off · lay on · lay out · lay over · lay up
entries.see also: inlay, mislay, overlay, underlay, waylay, lie

entries.meaning: To create or produce something — and, in its many extended uses, to force, earn, reach, amount to, or manage something.
examples: I make coffee before anyone else in the house is up.
He made the whole dinner out of what was in the fridge.
That factory has made the same part since 1962.
That story makes me laugh every single time.
They made him apologize in front of the class.
Nobody has made her change her mind yet.
The new lights make the room feel twice as big.
The board made her chief financial officer.
Two years abroad had made him almost unrecognizable.
She makes more than both of us combined.
He made a fortune on that one contract.
They have made nothing on the store in three years.
Try not to make the same mistake twice.
They made three offers on the same house.
The team has made real progress this quarter.
Four quarters make a dollar.
With Dave, that makes nine people in a six-person van.
The last donation made it an even ten thousand.
If we leave now we can make the six o'clock train.
He made it to the hospital with ten minutes to spare.
She has made every practice this season.
He made up the entire story on the drive over.
They fought for a week and then made up.
Volunteers make up most of the staff.
She has made up for the missed weeks with extra hours.
I can barely make out the signature.
We made out fine without the generator.
Nobody has made out what the last line of the letter says.
We'll make do with what's in the pantry.
They made do on one income for years.
He has made do without a car since he moved downtown.
The crowd made for the exits as soon as it started raining.
Thin walls make for awkward conversations.
Someone had made off with the tip jar.
Make up your mind — the table is only held until seven.
She had made up her mind long before the meeting started.

senses.head: Create, produce, build
body: The core sense: bringing something into existence, from a sandwich to a spacecraft. (делать, изготавливать, производить)
examples: I make coffee before anyone else in the house is up.
He made the whole dinner out of what was in the fridge.
That factory has made the same part since 1962.

senses.head: Force or cause someone to do something
body: Active make takes a bare infinitive — they made him apologize — but the passive takes to: he was made to apologize, never ✗ he was made apologize. (заставлять, вынуждать)
examples: That story makes me laugh every single time.
They made him apologize in front of the class.
Nobody has made her change her mind yet.

senses.head: Cause to become; appoint
body: Make + object + adjective (make me happy) or + noun (make her chairman). The appointing use is formal. (делать (каким-л.), превращать; назначать)
examples: The new lights make the room feel twice as big.
The board made her chief financial officer.
Two years abroad had made him almost unrecognizable.

senses.head: Earn money
body: Make a living, make money, make sixty thousand a year. Completely neutral in American English, where earn sounds more formal. (зарабатывать)
examples: She makes more than both of us combined.
He made a fortune on that one contract.
They have made nothing on the store in three years.

senses.head: Light verb: make a decision, a mistake, an offer
body: Make carries dozens of fixed noun combinations where it means little more than 'do': make a decision, a mistake, an effort, a promise, a call, progress, an offer. Learn them as units. (совершать, принимать, делать (в устойчивых сочетаниях))
examples: Try not to make the same mistake twice.
They made three offers on the same house.
The team has made real progress this quarter.

senses.head: Amount to, equal
body: Arithmetic and totals: two and two make four, that makes eleven of us. (составлять, равняться)
examples: Four quarters make a dollar.
With Dave, that makes nine people in a six-person van.
The last donation made it an even ten thousand.

senses.head: Reach, arrive at, manage to attend
body: Make the train, make the deadline, make it to the airport. Very often with it: we made it. (успевать, добираться, поспевать)
examples: If we leave now we can make the six o'clock train.
He made it to the hospital with ten minutes to spare.
She has made every practice this season.

senses.head: Make up — invent, reconcile, or constitute
body: Three unrelated meanings share one phrase: invent a story, end a quarrel, and form the whole of something (volunteers make up most of the staff). Make up for means compensate. (выдумывать; мириться; составлять)
examples: He made up the entire story on the drive over.
They fought for a week and then made up.
Volunteers make up most of the staff.
She has made up for the missed weeks with extra hours.

senses.head: Make out — discern, or manage
body: To make out a shape or a signature is to perceive it with difficulty; how did you make out? asks how you did. In American slang it also means to kiss at length. (разобрать (разглядеть, расслышать); справляться)
examples: I can barely make out the signature.
We made out fine without the generator.
Nobody has made out what the last line of the letter says.

senses.head: Make do — manage with what's available
body: A fixed phrase, always make do (with). There is no ✗ make due. (обходиться (тем, что есть))
examples: We'll make do with what's in the pantry.
They made do on one income for years.
He has made do without a car since he moved downtown.

senses.head: Make for; make off with
body: Make for a place means head toward it, and make for + noun also means produce a result (that makes for a long day). Make off with something means steal it and go. (направляться к; способствовать; удрать (с чем-л.))
examples: The crowd made for the exits as soon as it started raining.
Thin walls make for awkward conversations.
Someone had made off with the tip jar.

senses.head: Make up one's mind — decide
body: A fixed idiom separate from the other make up senses: to arrive at a decision, often after hesitating. (решаться, принимать решение)
examples: Make up your mind — the table is only held until seven.
She had made up her mind long before the meeting started.

entries.register: everyday — one of the handful of verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: In the "force someone to" sense, active make takes a bare infinitive but the passive takes to: They made him apologize becomes He was made to apologize — ✗ He was made apologize. Note also that made is a homophone of maid.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the creating, forcing, earning, and light-verb senses (make a mistake, make a living). The amount to sense is stative and copula-like, joining subject to a complement rather than acting on an object: four quarters make a dollar, that makes nine of us — no progressive, ✗ four quarters are making a dollar.
entries.transitivity: both, and mostly transitive — plain transitive (make coffee), ditransitive (make her a sandwich), and complex-transitive with a complement (make her chairman, make me happy) or a bare infinitive (they made him apologize). Intransitive only inside the fixed make do and make for.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the same part has been made there since 1962; she was made chief financial officer. Note the shift in the forcing sense: the passive requires to — he was made to apologize, ✗ he was made apologize. No passive of the amount to sense: ✗ A dollar is made by four quarters.
entries.phrasal verbs: make for · make of · make off · make off with · make out · make over · make up · make up for · make up to

entries.meaning: To put something down somewhere and forget where it went — to misplace it temporarily.
examples: I mislay my glasses about twice a day.
He mislaid the tickets somewhere between the car and the gate.
She has mislaid the spare key again.
The office had mislaid my file, so I filled the form out twice.
He mislays his phone constantly but always finds it by dinner.

senses.head: Misplace, lose track of
body: Narrower than lose: what you mislay is expected to turn up. Slightly formal in American English, where misplace is the everyday word; mislay is commoner in British usage. (класть не на место, затерять)
examples: I mislay my glasses about twice a day.
He mislaid the tickets somewhere between the car and the gate.
She has mislaid the spare key again.
The office had mislaid my file, so I filled the form out twice.
He mislays his phone constantly but always finds it by dinner.

entries.register: rare — American English reaches for misplace; mislay is chiefly British
entries.contrast: Forms follow lay exactly. The meaning is narrower than lose: to mislay something is to put it somewhere and forget where, with the expectation that it will turn up. You mislay your keys; you lose your job.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and narrower than lose: to put something down and forget where, with the expectation that it turns up.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — mislay your glasses, mislay the tickets. ✗ He mislaid again is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes — my file had been mislaid by the office, so I filled the form out twice; the spare key has been mislaid again.

entries.meaning: To spill over the edge of a container, or to be too full to hold everything that is in it.
examples: The gutters overflow every time it rains hard.
The tub overflowed while I was on the phone.
The creek has overflowed its banks twice this spring.
By dawn the river had overflowed the levee at three points.
Her inbox overflows by Monday afternoon.
The meeting overflowed into the hallway.
The shelter has overflowed every night this winter.
She overflows with enthusiasm for every new project.
His letter overflowed with apologies.
The town has overflowed with visitors since the film came out.
The counter overflows after 65,535 events.
The input overflowed the buffer and crashed the service.
Attackers had overflowed the stack to run code of their own.

senses.head: Spill over the edge
body: Of liquid and of the things that hold it. Regular in modern American English: ✗ the sink has overflown should be has overflowed — overflown belongs to overfly. (переливаться через край, выходить из берегов)
examples: The gutters overflow every time it rains hard.
The tub overflowed while I was on the phone.
The creek has overflowed its banks twice this spring.
By dawn the river had overflowed the levee at three points.

senses.head: Be too full; spill into another space
body: Of a room, a container, or a schedule that cannot hold what it is given. Often overflow into, meaning the surplus goes somewhere else. (переполняться, не вмещаться)
examples: Her inbox overflows by Monday afternoon.
The meeting overflowed into the hallway.
The shelter has overflowed every night this winter.

senses.head: Be filled with feeling
body: Figurative and warm, usually in the -ing form: overflowing with gratitude, overflowing with enthusiasm. (быть переполненным (чувством))
examples: She overflows with enthusiasm for every new project.
His letter overflowed with apologies.
The town has overflowed with visitors since the film came out.

senses.head: Exceed capacity (computing)
body: Technical: when a value or a memory buffer exceeds the space allotted to it. Buffer overflow is the standard security term. (переполняться (о буфере, счётчике))
examples: The counter overflows after 65,535 events.
The input overflowed the buffer and crashed the service.
Attackers had overflowed the stack to run code of their own.

entries.forms: overflow /ˌoʊvərˈfloʊ/ · overflowed /ˌoʊvərˈfloʊd/ · overflowed /ˌoʊvərˈfloʊd/ — the source list records the old strong participle overflown /ˌoʊvərˈfloʊn/
entries.register: everyday — sinks, rivers, and parking lots overflow in ordinary speech
entries.contrast: In current American English overflow is a plain regular verb: ✗ The sink has overflown should be The sink has overflowed. The form overflown does exist, but it belongs to a different verb — overfly, to fly over: the border has been overflown by drones. The verb is oh-ver-FLOH; the noun (an overflow pipe) is OH-ver-floh /ˈoʊvərˌfloʊ/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and mostly a process rather than a deed: liquid spilling over (the tub overflowed), a space too full (the meeting overflowed into the hallway), feeling brimming over (overflowing with gratitude), and a buffer exceeding its space.
entries.transitivity: both — normally intransitive, often with into (the shelter has overflowed every night), but transitive with the thing exceeded as object: the creek overflowed its banks, the input overflowed the buffer.
entries.passive: restricted — no passive at all of the intransitive the tub overflowed. The transitive passive is standard only in computing and security writing: the stack had been overflowed to run code. With banks and levees it is marginal: ? the levee was overflowed at three points.

entries.meaning: To cover a surface with a layer, or to place one layer, image, or set of data on top of another.
examples: Designers overlay the street map with live traffic data.
The app overlays subtitles on the video automatically.
The engineer has overlaid the new route on the old survey.
Craftsmen overlay the cheap wood with walnut veneer.
The artist overlaid the photograph with gold leaf.
Someone had overlaid the panel with a thin sheet of copper.
Politics overlays even the smallest decision here.
Later editors overlaid the text with commentary of their own.
Nostalgia has overlaid every memory he has of that summer.

senses.head: Place one image or layer over another
body: Graphics, mapping, and video: putting one layer on top of another so that both remain visible. This is the everyday modern sense. (накладывать (изображение, слой))
examples: Designers overlay the street map with live traffic data.
The app overlays subtitles on the video automatically.
The engineer has overlaid the new route on the old survey.

senses.head: Cover with a layer of material
body: Physical coating or facing — gold leaf, copper, veneer — and often passive: the dome is overlaid with gold. Careful: the form overlay is also the past tense of overlie, which means to lie on top of. (покрывать (слоем), облицовывать)
examples: Craftsmen overlay the cheap wood with walnut veneer.
The artist overlaid the photograph with gold leaf.
Someone had overlaid the panel with a thin sheet of copper.

senses.head: Impose a quality on top of something
body: Figurative: a tone, a meaning, or a later influence added over an original. Formal and mostly written. (накладывать отпечаток, привносить (поверх))
examples: Politics overlays even the smallest decision here.
Later editors overlaid the text with commentary of their own.
Nostalgia has overlaid every memory he has of that summer.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in design, mapping, and technical writing, less common in speech
entries.contrast: Overlay is the transitive verb — you overlay one thing on another — and gives overlaid. Its lookalike overlie means to lie on top of and gives overlay, overlain, so the word overlay is simultaneously a present tense and someone else's past tense: the shale overlay the coal is overlie, not overlay. The noun shifts stress to OH-ver-lay /ˈoʊvərˌleɪ/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: putting one layer, image, or data set on top of another (overlay the map with traffic data), coating a surface (overlay the wood with veneer), and the figurative politics overlays every decision here.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory, in the frame overlay A with B or overlay B on A. Careful: the intransitive-looking the shale overlay the coal is the past of a different verb, overlie.
entries.passive: yes, and very common in the coating sense — the dome is overlaid with gold leaf; the new route has been overlaid on the old survey.

entries.meaning: To pay more than something is worth, more than a person's work is worth, or more than the amount actually owed.
examples: Tourists always overpay for cabs from the airport.
The city overpaid the contractor by nearly a million dollars.
We have overpaid on this lease for two years running.
Fans think the club overpays its whole back line.
The board overpaid two executives for years.
Critics say the league has overpaid for a player past his prime.
If you overpay, the balance rolls into next month.
He realized he had overpaid only after he saw the receipt.
Thousands of filers have overpaid their estimated taxes this year.

senses.head: Pay too much for something
body: The everyday sense, with the goods or the seller as the object. Follows pay: the past and participle are overpaid, never ✗ overpayed. (переплачивать (за что-л.))
examples: Tourists always overpay for cabs from the airport.
The city overpaid the contractor by nearly a million dollars.
We have overpaid on this lease for two years running.

senses.head: Pay a person more than the work is worth
body: Of salaries, and usually a complaint. The participle doubles as an adjective: an overpaid executive. (платить (кому-л.) сверх меры)
examples: Fans think the club overpays its whole back line.
The board overpaid two executives for years.
Critics say the league has overpaid for a player past his prime.

senses.head: Pay more than is due
body: Accounting and tax: an amount above what was owed, which then comes back as a refund or a credit. (переплатить (сверх причитающегося))
examples: If you overpay, the balance rolls into next month.
He realized he had overpaid only after he saw the receipt.
Thousands of filers have overpaid their estimated taxes this year.

entries.register: everyday — we overpaid for the house is plain American conversation
entries.contrast: Nothing tricky — it is pay with a prefix, so the past and participle are overpaid, never ✗ overpayed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: paying more than a thing is worth (overpay for cabs), more than a person's work is worth (overpay its back line), or more than is actually owed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the seller, worker, or amount as object (the city overpaid the contractor), intransitive when the object is understood (tourists always overpay, if you overpay, the balance rolls over).
entries.passive: yes with a person or a sum as object — two executives were overpaid for years; the contractor was overpaid by nearly a million dollars. The participle is a standard adjective: an overpaid executive. No passive of the intransitive we overpaid for the house.

entries.meaning: To give money for goods, work, or a debt — and, in its wider senses, to be worth doing, to suffer for something, or to give what is owed in attention and respect.
examples: I pay the rent on the first of every month.
He paid cash for the whole thing.
We had paid for the tickets before the show sold out.
She pays her credit card in full every month.
The company paid its fine without appealing.
They have paid off the car loan early.
The restaurant pays its servers weekly.
They paid her more than she asked for.
The district has paid substitutes late three times this year.
It pays to read the fine print.
The store never really paid.
Patience has paid for them more than once.
You'll pay for that remark.
He paid for the sprint with two days of sore legs.
The team has paid dearly for that one bad trade.
She pays attention to details nobody else notices.
He paid her a real compliment for once.
Thousands have paid their respects at the memorial.
The bond pays four percent a year.
That fund paid nothing for two straight quarters.
The account has paid interest every quarter since 2019.
All that studying has paid off.
The extra rehearsal really paid off.
Someone had paid off the inspector.
I'll pay you back on Friday.
He paid them back by leaking the memo.
She has paid back every dollar she borrowed.
The policy pays out only after a thirty-day wait.
The insurer paid out less than half the claim.
They payed out the anchor chain slowly.

senses.head: Give money for goods or work
body: The core sense. The y becomes i in the past: paid, never ✗ payed. (платить, оплачивать)
examples: I pay the rent on the first of every month.
He paid cash for the whole thing.
We had paid for the tickets before the show sold out.

senses.head: Settle a debt or a bill
body: Pay a bill, pay a loan, pay taxes, pay a fine. With off, it means clear the debt completely. (погашать (долг), рассчитываться)
examples: She pays her credit card in full every month.
The company paid its fine without appealing.
They have paid off the car loan early.

senses.head: Pay someone wages
body: With a person as the object, and two objects are normal: pay him forty dollars. (платить (кому-л.), выплачивать зарплату)
examples: The restaurant pays its servers weekly.
They paid her more than she asked for.
The district has paid substitutes late three times this year.

senses.head: Be profitable, be worth doing
body: No object: it pays to arrive early, crime doesn't pay, the store never really paid. (окупаться, быть выгодным)
examples: It pays to read the fine print.
The store never really paid.
Patience has paid for them more than once.

senses.head: Suffer the consequences
body: Pay for a mistake, pay the price, you'll pay for this. Nothing to do with money — this is threat or moral reckoning. (поплатиться, расплачиваться)
examples: You'll pay for that remark.
He paid for the sprint with two days of sore legs.
The team has paid dearly for that one bad trade.

senses.head: Give what is owed: attention, respects, a visit
body: A fixed set of combinations where nothing is bought: pay attention, pay a compliment, pay a visit, pay your respects, pay tribute. (оказывать, уделять (внимание, почтение))
examples: She pays attention to details nobody else notices.
He paid her a real compliment for once.
Thousands have paid their respects at the memorial.

senses.head: Yield a return (finance)
body: Of a bond, a stock, or an account: to produce interest or a dividend at a stated rate. (приносить доход, давать проценты)
examples: The bond pays four percent a year.
That fund paid nothing for two straight quarters.
The account has paid interest every quarter since 2019.

senses.head: Pay off — succeed after effort, or bribe
body: Beyond clearing a debt, pay off means an effort produced its reward — and, quite separately, that someone was bribed into silence. (оправдать себя, принести плоды; дать взятку)
examples: All that studying has paid off.
The extra rehearsal really paid off.
Someone had paid off the inspector.

senses.head: Pay back — return money, or retaliate
body: Money returned to the person who lent it, or, figuratively, revenge: pay someone back for something. (возвращать (долг); отплатить, отомстить)
examples: I'll pay you back on Friday.
He paid them back by leaking the memo.
She has paid back every dollar she borrowed.

senses.head: Pay out — disburse money, or let out rope
body: Of an insurer or a bet, to hand the money over. In the nautical sense of letting a rope run out, the spelling of the past really is payed — the one place that spelling is correct. (выплачивать (страховку); травить (канат))
examples: The policy pays out only after a thirty-day wait.
The insurer paid out less than half the claim.
They payed out the anchor chain slowly.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The y becomes i in the past: paid, not ✗ payed. The spelling payed is real but nautical only — you pay out a rope and you payed it out. For money, favors, compliments and attention, it is always paid.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: handing over money (pay the rent), settling a debt, giving what is owed in attention or respect (pay attention, pay a visit), suffering consequences (you'll pay for that), and yielding a return (the bond pays four percent).
entries.transitivity: ditransitive at its core — they paid her more than she asked for, pay him forty dollars — and plain transitive with either object alone (pay the fine, pay the servers). Intransitive in the 'be profitable' sense: it pays to read the fine print, the store never really paid.
entries.passive: yes, with the recipient as the natural passive subject — the servers are paid weekly, she was paid more than she asked for; the sum promotes too: the fine was paid without appeal. No passive of the profitable sense: ✗ It is paid to read the fine print.
entries.phrasal verbs: pay back · pay down · pay for · pay off · pay out · pay up

entries.meaning: To pay for something before you receive or use it, or to pay off a loan ahead of schedule.
examples: Guests can prepay the room online and skip the front desk.
We prepaid the shipping so nobody gets a bill at the door.
The company has prepaid next year's insurance in full.
The service prepays the postage on every return label.
You may prepay the mortgage at any time without a penalty.
They prepaid the last two years of the note.
He had prepaid the property taxes, so the notice was an error.

senses.head: Pay in advance
body: Standard for postage, shipping, hotel rooms, and phone service. The participle is very common as an adjective — a prepaid card — and there the stress moves forward to PREE-paid. (платить вперёд, оплачивать заранее)
examples: Guests can prepay the room online and skip the front desk.
We prepaid the shipping so nobody gets a bill at the door.
The company has prepaid next year's insurance in full.
The service prepays the postage on every return label.

senses.head: Pay off a loan early
body: Finance: to repay principal before it comes due. Some contracts charge a prepayment penalty for doing it. (досрочно погашать (кредит))
examples: You may prepay the mortgage at any time without a penalty.
They prepaid the last two years of the note.
He had prepaid the property taxes, so the notice was an error.

entries.register: everyday — gas pumps, shipping labels, and hotel bookings all ask you to prepay
entries.contrast: Follows pay. The participle has largely turned into an adjective — a prepaid card, a prepaid envelope — and when it does, the stress moves forward: PREE-paid /ˈpriˌpeɪd/ as an adjective, pree-PAID as a verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: paying before you receive or use something (prepay the room), or paying off a loan ahead of schedule (prepay the mortgage).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the thing paid for as object (we prepaid the shipping), and the object drops freely when it is obvious (guests can prepay online).
entries.passive: yes — next year's insurance has been prepaid in full; the postage is prepaid on every return label. The participle is far commoner as an adjective, with stress on the first syllable: a prepaid card.

entries.meaning: To make something again in a new form — a film, a kitchen, a career.
examples: Studios remake the same three movies over and over.
The director remade his own film for an American audience.
Hollywood has remade that thriller twice already.
She remakes her budget from scratch every January.
They remade the kitchen in a single weekend.
Crews have remade the whole intersection since June.
Every new dean tries to remake the college in his own image.
He remade himself completely after the divorce.
Two elections have remade the party from the ground up.

senses.head: Make a new version of a film or song
body: The commonest modern use. Stress separates verb from noun: ree-MAYK the film, then watch the REE-mayk. (снимать ремейк, переделывать (фильм, песню))
examples: Studios remake the same three movies over and over.
The director remade his own film for an American audience.
Hollywood has remade that thriller twice already.

senses.head: Rebuild, redo from scratch
body: Of physical things and plans: to make something over completely rather than repair it. (переделывать, перестраивать)
examples: She remakes her budget from scratch every January.
They remade the kitchen in a single weekend.
Crews have remade the whole intersection since June.

senses.head: Transform, reinvent (a person or institution)
body: Figurative and often grand: remake himself, remake the party, remake society. (преображать, перекраивать)
examples: Every new dean tries to remake the college in his own image.
He remade himself completely after the divorce.
Two elections have remade the party from the ground up.

entries.register: everyday — films, kitchens, and careers all get remade in ordinary conversation
entries.contrast: Follows make. Stress separates the verb from the noun: ree-MAYK is the verb, REE-mayk /ˈriˌmeɪk/ is the noun — they remade the film versus the remake was terrible.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: making a new version of a film or song, rebuilding something from scratch (remake the kitchen), or transforming a person or institution (remake the party).
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — ✗ Studios remake constantly needs an object. The reflexive is normal in the transforming sense: he remade himself after the divorce.
entries.passive: yes — that thriller has been remade twice already; the whole intersection has been remade since June; the party was remade from the ground up.

entries.meaning: To pay money back, to return a kindness — or, in a bitter twist on the same frame, to return an injury.
examples: I'll repay you on Friday, I promise.
He repaid the loan in eighteen months.
She has repaid every dollar she borrowed from her sister.
I don't know how to repay your kindness.
They repaid the neighbors with a week of free babysitting.
By spring they had repaid every favor the family had done them.
He repaid their trust with a lawsuit.
History has repaid that generosity poorly.
Nothing repays effort quite like daily practice.
The archive repaid three days of digging.
The detour has repaid us with the best view on the trip.

senses.head: Pay back money owed
body: You repay a person or a loan; you pay back money to someone. Follows pay: repaid, never ✗ repayed. (возвращать долг, выплачивать)
examples: I'll repay you on Friday, I promise.
He repaid the loan in eighteen months.
She has repaid every dollar she borrowed from her sister.

senses.head: Return a favor or kindness
body: The object can be the person or the kindness itself: repay her generosity, repay him for his patience. (отблагодарить, отплатить (добром))
examples: I don't know how to repay your kindness.
They repaid the neighbors with a week of free babysitting.
By spring they had repaid every favor the family had done them.

senses.head: Requite with harm
body: Formal, and almost always in the frame repay X with Y, where Y is worse than X deserved. (отплатить (злом), воздать)
examples: He repaid their trust with a lawsuit.
History has repaid that generosity poorly.

senses.head: Be worth the effort
body: Formal and written, with a thing as the subject: the book repays careful reading. (оправдывать (усилия), вознаграждать)
examples: Nothing repays effort quite like daily practice.
The archive repaid three days of digging.
The detour has repaid us with the best view on the trip.

entries.register: everyday — you repay a loan or a favor without sounding bookish
entries.contrast: Follows pay: repaid, never ✗ repayed. Watch the pattern of objects — you repay a person, a loan, or a kindness, but you pay back money to someone.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: returning money (repay the loan), returning a kindness (repay your generosity), requiting with harm (repay their trust with a lawsuit), and — with a thing as subject — being worth the effort (the book repays careful reading).
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — the object may be the person (I'll repay you), the debt (repay the loan), or the kindness. Marginally ditransitive (repay him the money); the usual frames are repay X for Y and repay X with Y.
entries.passive: yes in the money and favor senses — the loan was repaid in eighteen months; every favor the family had done them had been repaid. Restricted in the 'be worth the effort' sense: ? Careful reading is repaid by the book is awkward.

entries.meaning: To put something into words — and, by extension, what a text indicates, what people report, and what a thing conveys without speaking.
examples: Don't say anything until the lawyer gets here.
She said she would call back after lunch.
He has said the same thing in every meeting this month.
The sign says the pool closes at nine.
The letter said nothing about a deadline.
The forecast has said rain all week.
They say the pass is closed until May.
He is said to have turned down the job twice.
Nobody had said a word about the layoffs.
Say it rains on Saturday — what's the backup plan?
Let's say fifty people show up.
Say you're right; it still doesn't help us.
He says grace before every meal.
She said a few words at the service.
The priest has said mass in that chapel for thirty years.
The fact that he left early says everything.
Her silence said more than an argument would have.
That one decision has said more about the company than any press release.
Just say the word and I'll book it.
If you'd wanted help, you should have said so.
He never said so out loud, but everyone knew.

senses.head: Utter words, speak
body: The basic verb of speech. Watch the objects: you say something to someone, but you tell someone something — ✗ He said me the news. (говорить, сказать, произносить)
examples: Don't say anything until the lawyer gets here.
She said she would call back after lunch.
He has said the same thing in every meeting this month.

senses.head: Of a text, sign, or instrument: indicate
body: With an inanimate subject: what a written or displayed thing conveys. The sign says, my watch says nine, the label says dry clean only. (гласить; показывать (о надписи, приборе))
examples: The sign says the pool closes at nine.
The letter said nothing about a deadline.
The forecast has said rain all week.

senses.head: Report, claim (they say, is said to)
body: The impersonal report of common belief. The passive frame is said to is formal and standard in journalism. (говорят, утверждают; считается)
examples: They say the pass is closed until May.
He is said to have turned down the job twice.
Nobody had said a word about the layoffs.

senses.head: Suppose, assume (let's say)
body: Used to set up a hypothetical or an estimate: say it rains — then what?, let's say fifty people. Imperative in form, and fixed. (допустим, скажем, предположим)
examples: Say it rains on Saturday — what's the backup plan?
Let's say fifty people show up.
Say you're right; it still doesn't help us.

senses.head: Recite (a prayer, a line, a word)
body: Say grace, say a prayer, say your lines, say a few words. Also used of pronouncing a word: say it in Russian. (произносить, читать (молитву, реплику))
examples: He says grace before every meal.
She said a few words at the service.
The priest has said mass in that chapel for thirty years.

senses.head: Convey, mean (what something says about you)
body: Of art, evidence, or behavior — what it communicates without words. That says a lot about him. (выражать, свидетельствовать, говорить о (чём-л.))
examples: The fact that he left early says everything.
Her silence said more than an argument would have.
That one decision has said more about the company than any press release.

senses.head: Say so; say the word
body: Two fixed uses: say so means state it openly (if you don't like it, say so), and just say the word means give the signal and it will happen. (сказать прямо; дать знать)
examples: Just say the word and I'll book it.
If you'd wanted help, you should have said so.
He never said so out loud, but everyone knew.

entries.register: everyday — one of the commonest verbs in the language
entries.contrast: The spelling adds -d like paid, but the sound does not follow. Say rhymes with day; said rhymes with bed, not with paid; and says rhymes with fez, not with pays. Separately, say and tell split by object: you say something to someone but you tell someone something — ✗ He said me the news.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, the basic verb of speech (say something), extended to what a text or instrument indicates (the sign says the pool closes at nine), to reported common belief (they say the pass is closed), and to what something conveys (her silence said more than an argument).
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is normally a clause (she said she would call back) or a noun (say nothing, say grace). Never ditransitive: the addressee takes to — say something to someone, ✗ He said me the news (that frame belongs to tell).
entries.passive: yes — nothing was said about a deadline; and the impersonal raising passive is standard journalism: he is said to have turned down the job twice. The addressee can never be the passive subject: ✗ I was said the news.

entries.meaning: To travel over snow on skis — and, transitively, to ski a particular run or mountain.
examples: We ski every weekend in January.
She has skied in both Colorado and Utah.
My father still skis at seventy-two.
They skied the back bowls all afternoon.
He had never skied that face before the trip to Vermont.
She skis the same three runs every time.

senses.head: Travel on skis
body: Both the sport and the means of travel, with no object needed. Skied here is /skid/, rhyming with seed — the identical spelling from sky is /skaɪd/. (кататься на лыжах, ходить на лыжах)
examples: We ski every weekend in January.
She has skied in both Colorado and Utah.
My father still skis at seventy-two.

senses.head: Ski a particular run or mountain
body: Transitive and completely standard among skiers: ski the back bowls, ski the moguls, ski a black diamond. (спускаться (по склону), проходить трассу)
examples: They skied the back bowls all afternoon.
He had never skied that face before the trip to Vermont.
She skis the same three runs every time.

entries.register: everyday — the plain American verb for the sport, wherever there is snow
entries.third person: skis (not ✗ skies) · -ing form: skiing (both i's stay)
entries.contrast: Skied from ski is pronounced /skid/, rhyming with seed. Spelled identically is skied /skaɪd/ from sky, a baseball verb meaning to hit the ball high — he skied it to center field. Only context tells them apart. Note also the plural noun skis, never skies, which belongs to sky.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: traveling over snow on skis, both as the sport and as a means of getting somewhere.
entries.transitivity: both — normally intransitive with no object at all (we ski every weekend, my father still skis at seventy-two), transitive with a run or a mountain as object (they skied the back bowls, ski a black diamond).
entries.passive: restricted — no passive of the intransitive we ski every weekend. The transitive passive is possible but confined to skiers' talk: that face had never been skied before that winter.

entries.meaning: To put a layer of something underneath, usually to support or cushion what sits on top.
examples: Installers underlay hardwood floors with a thin foam sheet.
They underlaid the carpet with thick padding.
The crew has underlaid the whole second floor with cork.
The pad underlays the rug so it doesn't slide on the wood.
The editor underlaid the new words under the same melody.
Someone had underlaid the tile with the wrong material entirely.
A thin steel plate underlays the whole mechanism.

senses.head: Put a layer underneath
body: Flooring and construction: foam, cork, or padding laid under a finished surface. Careful — underlay is also the past tense of underlie: the assumptions that underlay the plan is that other verb. (подстилать, подкладывать)
examples: Installers underlay hardwood floors with a thin foam sheet.
They underlaid the carpet with thick padding.
The crew has underlaid the whole second floor with cork.
The pad underlays the rug so it doesn't slide on the wood.

senses.head: Support or set beneath (technical)
body: Of anything placed under something else for support — including packing set under type in printing, and lyrics set under a melody in music. Formal and uncommon. (подкреплять снизу, служить подложкой)
examples: The editor underlaid the new words under the same melody.
Someone had underlaid the tile with the wrong material entirely.
A thin steel plate underlays the whole mechanism.

entries.register: rare — a flooring-trade verb; most Americans know only the noun, the padding under a carpet
entries.contrast: The same collision as overlay: underlay is the transitive verb giving underlaid, but it is also the past tense of underlie, which gives underlay, underlain. The assumptions that underlay the plan is underlie. The noun — the padding under a carpet — is UN-der-lay /ˈʌndərˌleɪ/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: putting a layer of something underneath for support or cushioning (underlay the carpet with padding), including the technical printing and music uses.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory, in the frame underlay A with B. Careful: the assumptions that underlay the plan is the past of a different verb, underlie.
entries.passive: yes — the carpet was underlaid with thick padding; the tile had been underlaid with the wrong material entirely; the whole second floor has been underlaid with cork.

entries.meaning: To pay someone less than their work is worth, or to pay less than the amount owed.
examples: Some restaurants underpay their kitchen staff badly.
The company underpaid her for three years before she noticed.
The district has underpaid substitute teachers for a decade.
If you underpay your estimated taxes, you owe a penalty.
Auditors found that the firm had underpaid dozens of workers.
That chain routinely underpays its payroll taxes.

senses.head: Pay someone too little
body: Of wages and of workers. The participle is the standard adjective, fixed in overworked and underpaid. (недоплачивать, мало платить)
examples: Some restaurants underpay their kitchen staff badly.
The company underpaid her for three years before she noticed.
The district has underpaid substitute teachers for a decade.

senses.head: Pay less than the amount due
body: Accounting and tax: a shortfall against what was owed, usually corrected later with interest or a penalty. (уплатить не полностью, внести меньше должного)
examples: If you underpay your estimated taxes, you owe a penalty.
Auditors found that the firm had underpaid dozens of workers.
That chain routinely underpays its payroll taxes.

entries.register: everyday — wage talk uses it constantly, fixed in overworked and underpaid
entries.contrast: Follows pay. The participle doubles as an adjective, and there it is the standard way to describe a job: overworked and underpaid.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: paying a worker less than the work is worth (underpay the kitchen staff), or paying less than the amount actually due (underpay your estimated taxes).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the worker or the amount as object (the company underpaid her for three years), intransitive when the object is understood (if you underpay, you owe a penalty).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the commoner form — substitute teachers have been underpaid for a decade; dozens of workers had been underpaid. The participle is the standard adjective in overworked and underpaid.

entries.meaning: To undo what was made — take it apart, destroy it, or strip a person of the standing that made them.
examples: Time has unmade the treaty piece by piece.
War had unmade the city long before he ever saw it.
What the legislature makes, the legislature unmakes.
A single scandal can unmake a career.
The new council unmade almost everything the last one built.
The same voters who made him have unmade him.
He left the bed unmade again.
The cabin sits at the end of an unmade road.

senses.head: Undo, destroy what was made
body: Formal and largely literary; ordinary speech uses undo or tear down. The classic frame pairs it with make. (разрушать, уничтожать (созданное))
examples: Time has unmade the treaty piece by piece.
War had unmade the city long before he ever saw it.
What the legislature makes, the legislature unmakes.

senses.head: Ruin or depose a person
body: Of reputations and careers: to destroy the position someone was given. Almost always set against make: the press can make or unmake a candidate. (губить, низвергать (кого-л.))
examples: A single scandal can unmake a career.
The new council unmade almost everything the last one built.
The same voters who made him have unmade him.

senses.head: Unmade — adjective: never made up
body: The participle is far commoner as a plain adjective, and there it means 'not made in the first place' — an unmade bed, an unmade road — nearly the opposite of the verb. (незастеленная (о постели); незавершённый)
examples: He left the bed unmade again.
The cabin sits at the end of an unmade road.

entries.register: rare — formal and mostly literary; speech says undo or tear down
entries.contrast: Follows make, but the participle is far commoner as a plain adjective with a different sense: an unmade bed is one that was never made, not one that someone un-made. The verb itself is formal and mostly literary.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but formal and largely literary: undoing what was made (time has unmade the treaty) or destroying a person's standing (a scandal can unmake a career).
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory, and typically set against make: what the legislature makes, the legislature unmakes.
entries.passive: yes, though context has to carry it — the treaty was unmade piece by piece; he was unmade by the same voters who made him. Beware the ordinary adjective: the bed was unmade means it was never made, not that someone un-made it.

entries.meaning: To take back something you have said — usually invoked in the recognition that you cannot.
examples: You cannot unsay a thing like that.
No apology has unsaid the insult.
Once a rumor is out, nobody unsays it.
By the end of the hearing he had unsaid almost every claim in his statement.
She wished she could take it back, but she never unsaid a word of it.
Some things are better left unsaid.
The real reason went unsaid all evening.

senses.head: Take back words
body: Nearly always in a frame that admits it is impossible: you cannot unsay it, what's said cannot be unsaid. Unsaid rhymes with bed. (брать слова назад, отрекаться от сказанного)
examples: You cannot unsay a thing like that.
No apology has unsaid the insult.
Once a rumor is out, nobody unsays it.

senses.head: Retract a claim formally
body: Of statements on the record: to withdraw them. Rare and formal — American English usually says retract or walk back. (отказываться от своих слов, дезавуировать)
examples: By the end of the hearing he had unsaid almost every claim in his statement.
She wished she could take it back, but she never unsaid a word of it.

senses.head: Unsaid — adjective: left unspoken
body: By far the commonest use of the form, and it means 'never said at all' rather than 'taken back': some things are better left unsaid, it went unsaid. (невысказанный, недосказанный)
examples: Some things are better left unsaid.
The real reason went unsaid all evening.

entries.register: rare — the verb survives mostly in cannot be unsaid; only the adjective unsaid is everyday
entries.contrast: Follows say, including the vowel: unsaid rhymes with bed. Like unmade, the participle is far commoner as an adjective meaning "never said at all" — better left unsaid — which is nearly the opposite of the verb's sense of taking words back. The verb itself appears mostly in the fixed idea that something cannot be unsaid.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a speech act, but almost frozen in the recognition that it cannot be performed: you cannot unsay a thing like that.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — unsay a word, unsay every claim in his statement.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is where the verb actually lives — what's said cannot be unsaid; once a rumor is out, it is never unsaid. Note that the bare adjective unsaid means 'never spoken at all' — some things are better left unsaid — nearly the opposite.

entries.meaning: To lie in wait for someone and stop them on their way — historically to rob them, today usually just to corner them.
examples: Reporters waylay the senator outside the chamber every afternoon.
A neighbor waylaid me at the mailbox for twenty minutes.
Salespeople have waylaid him twice in the same parking lot.
She waylays me in the hallway whenever she needs a favor.
They planned to waylay the messenger before he reached the border.
Raiders waylaid the supply column at the pass.
Bandits had waylaid the coach on the mountain road.

senses.head: Intercept and detain someone
body: The everyday modern sense, mild and often faintly comic: catching someone as they pass and holding them up, usually in conversation. (перехватить, задержать (по дороге))
examples: Reporters waylay the senator outside the chamber every afternoon.
A neighbor waylaid me at the mailbox for twenty minutes.
Salespeople have waylaid him twice in the same parking lot.
She waylays me in the hallway whenever she needs a favor.

senses.head: Ambush, lie in wait to attack
body: The original sense — attacking a traveler on the road. It now sounds historical or literary rather than ordinary. (подстерегать, устраивать засаду)
examples: They planned to waylay the messenger before he reached the border.
Raiders waylaid the supply column at the pass.
Bandits had waylaid the coach on the mountain road.

entries.register: rare — recognized and faintly literary; ordinary speech says corner or hold up
entries.contrast: Forms follow lay. In modern American English the everyday sense is mild — to intercept someone and hold them up in conversation — while the older sense of ambushing a traveler to rob them now sounds historical.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: intercepting someone on their way, today usually just to corner them in conversation (waylay the senator outside the chamber), historically to ambush and rob them.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory and almost always a person — ✗ Reporters waylay every afternoon is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is at least as common as the active — I was waylaid at the mailbox for twenty minutes; the supply column was waylaid at the pass.
